title: The waterfall illusion
hook: Stare at a waterfall, then at the rocks, and the rocks seem to drift upwards.
peek: In 1834 a visitor to the Falls of Foyers in Scotland noticed that after watching the water, the nearby rocks appeared to climb. The waterfall illusion is a motion aftereffect, and it reveals how the brain measures movement.
lede: In 1834 Robert Addams published an account of a visit to the Falls of Foyers, near Loch Ness. After gazing at the falling water for a while, he looked at the rocks beside it and saw them moving upwards, against the flow. The effect, now called the motion aftereffect, is easy to repeat at any waterfall, or with a moving video and a still wall.

bullets.text: Addams was not the first to notice. Aristotle wrote that after watching a flowing river, still objects seem to move, but the Scottish waterfall gave the effect its popular name.

The usual explanation is adaptation. Brain cells tuned to downward motion fire steadily while you watch the water and gradually tire. When you turn to still rocks, upward-tuned cells briefly win out, so stillness reads as rising.
The illusion has an odd twist. The rocks seem to move, yet they never appear to change position. That suggests the brain judges motion and position with partly separate systems.
In the 19th century the Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau described a spiral version. After watching a rotating spiral that seems to expand, a still face or wall looks as if it is shrinking.
